A demoniac is a person believed to be possessed by a demon or evil spirit — meaning a malevolent supernatural being has taken up residence inside that person's body and is controlling or tormenting them from within.

The person themselves is the demoniac. Not the demon. The victim of the demon.
Who uses this word, and where does it appear?

This word lives almost entirely in three worlds:

1. Religious texts and scripture — especially the Christian Bible. The Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) describe Jesus encountering demoniacs and casting the possessing spirits out of them. This is the most famous context for the word. When you read a Bible translation or a commentary on it, "demoniac" is the standard English term for such a person.

2. Theology and religious scholarship — academic or theological writing about possession, exorcism, or the nature of evil spirits uses this word as a precise technical term.

3. Historical writing — historians writing about the medieval period, witch trials, or pre-modern medicine frequently use "demoniac" to describe how people in those eras categorized and labeled individuals with unexplained behavior.
What exactly is a demoniac experiencing?

In the belief systems where this word is used, a demoniac is not simply someone who believes in demons, or someone who is evil. The defining feature is involuntary possession — the person has been overtaken by an outside supernatural force against their will, or without their full consent.

This possession was believed to manifest as:

  • Violent, uncontrollable behavior
  • Superhuman physical strength
  • Speaking in strange voices or in languages the person doesn't know
  • Convulsions and seizures
  • Complete personality change
  • Apparent knowledge of hidden or supernatural things

The demoniac, in this framework, is essentially a battleground — a human being whose body and sometimes mind has been seized by something evil.
The demoniac vs. the demon: an important distinction

This is worth being crystal clear about:

  • The demon is the spirit — the supernatural evil entity.
  • The demoniac is the human being who is possessed by that demon.

So if you said "the priests confronted the demon," you'd be saying they faced the spirit. But if you said "the priests confronted the demoniac," you'd be saying they faced the afflicted person — the human host.
How does a demoniac get un-demoniaced?

The answer, in the traditions where this concept exists, is exorcism — a religious ritual, prayer, or command performed by a priest, holy person, or authority figure, ordering the demon to leave the person's body. Once successfully exorcised, the person is no longer a demoniac. They return to their normal self.

The most famous example: in the Gospels, when Jesus commands the spirits to leave the demoniac of the Gerasenes, the man — who had been violent, lived among tombs, and could not be restrained — immediately becomes calm, clothed, and in his right mind.
Why did people in the past call things "demonic possession"?

This is important context for understanding why "demoniac" appears so often in historical texts. Before modern medicine and psychiatry, many conditions that we now understand medically were completely mysterious:

  • Epilepsy (seizures, loss of control over the body)
  • Schizophrenia (hearing voices, altered reality)
  • Tourette's syndrome (involuntary movements and speech)
  • Severe dissociative disorders

People who displayed these symptoms were often labeled demoniacs, not out of cruelty (though cruelty sometimes followed), but because possession by an evil spirit was the only explanatory framework available. The demoniac label was, for its time, an attempt to make sense of something frightening and inexplicable.

This is why historians use the word non-judgmentally — they write "the woman was considered a demoniac by her community" as a neutral historical fact, not an endorsement of that belief.
The register and feel of the word

"Demoniac" as a noun is formal, old-fashioned, and specialized. You will not hear it in casual conversation. If someone today said "he's a demoniac," it would sound either deliberately archaic (like they're quoting scripture or writing historical fiction) or metaphorical and dramatic.

In everyday modern speech, the equivalent concept — if expressed at all — would be phrased as "a possessed person" or "someone undergoing demonic possession."
A few example sentences to cement it

• "The Gospel account describes the demoniac as so violent that no chain could hold him."
  • "Medieval inquisitors often conflated heretics with demoniacs, blurring the line between spiritual rebellion and supernatural affliction."
  • "After the exorcism, the demoniac reportedly sat quietly, recognizing his family for the first time in years."
  • "Historians now believe that many of the women accused of witchcraft were actually demoniacs in the eyes of their contemporaries — people seen as possessed rather than as willing servants of the devil."
The one-sentence definition you can always fall back on
A demoniac is a person believed to be inhabited and tormented or controlled by a demon — a human victim of supernatural possession, particularly in religious, historical, or scriptural contexts.
